events.text: A storyteller called Yeom Bak works the market with a wooden clapper. Today it is {llg_who}, who lived to {llg_told_age} and left {llg_thing} in {llg_region}, "not {llg_years} years gone, and my own grandmother swept its steps." He tells it nearly straight. You stay long after the coins have stopped, and you could not say why.

choices.text: Stay for the end and ask where it stands

effects.log: He tells you the road to {llg_region}, and he charges you for it. You remember the road anyway.

choices.text: Toss him a coin and go

effects.log: He bites it, nods and goes back to his clapper. The name stays in your head for the rest of the day, like a stone in a shoe.

events.text: "And when {llg_who} came to {llg_region}, the mountain itself knelt," says Yeom Bak, with both hands in the air. "So they built {llg_thing} on the spot where it knelt. {llg_He} lived to {llg_told_age}, and never once slept lying down." You find yourself thinking that nobody would be so stupid, and you are annoyed, and you cannot think why.

choices.text: Tell him that nobody could live that way

effects.log: "You have seen it, have you?" says Yeom Bak, and the crowd laughs. You had the oddest feeling, for a moment, that you had.

choices.text: Ask what they do at the hall these days

effects.log: They burn incense and ask for sons, he says, and rain. Most of it does not come. They go on asking.

events.text: Every province has its local god. {llg_region} has {llg_who}, a being of fire and patience who raised {llg_thing} in a single night some thousands of years ago, or so Yeom Bak swears. Children leave rice there. It has a birthday. Nobody, when you ask, has ever thought that {llg_he} might have had a mother.

choices.text: Ask whether {llg_he} ever had a mother

effects.log: They look at you as if you had asked whether the river has an uncle. You go home oddly lonely.

choices.text: Leave some rice next time you pass one of the little altars

effects.log: It is only rice. You are surprised at how careful you are to set it straight.

events.text: On the carters' map, {llg_landmark} has another name now. They call the height above it {llg_thing}, after {llg_who}, and an old carter who can remember being told about it says that {llg_he} died of {llg_cause}. He spits for luck. The name goes through you, for no reason, and you ask him to say it again.

choices.text: Ask him what {llg_he} was like

effects.log: "Short temper," says the carter. "Or tall. One of those." You laugh, and do not know why you are so pleased.

choices.text: Copy the name onto the back of your hand

effects.log: It washes off in a week. By then you have looked at it enough times.

events.text: Yeom Bak has a whole act about {llg_thing}. It seems {llg_who} once sat down there to rest, and the weight of {llg_his} sitting pressed the valley flat, and this is why the farming is good. The farmers, who are in the crowd, nod. {llg_He} also, it turns out, lived to {llg_told_age}.

choices.text: Ask a farmer whether anyone truly believes it

effects.log: "Of course not," he says, and then, more quietly, "We leave a share of the first barley, though."

choices.text: Laugh along with everyone

effects.log: You laugh harder than the joke deserves. You have the sense of someone having told a story about you at a party.

events.text: There is a very old rhyme for counting the mountains of {llg_region}, and every child knows it. {llg_Thing} is the third. It is only when you are nearly grown that you think to ask what the word means, and a grandmother tells you it is a word for a kind of giant, one of the old ones, from before the first emperor. It does not sound like a giant to you.

choices.text: Say the rhyme over to yourself until the word stops meaning anything

effects.log: It does not stop. You leave that for now. It will wait: it has waited this long.

choices.text: Go back to the skipping game

effects.log: You miss the rope on the third mountain. You always will now. The others find it very funny.

events.text: An old fighter at the inn has a limp and a story. He trained, he says, at {llg_thing} in {llg_region} under a teacher who trained under {llg_who} {llg_years} years gone. "Stones worn to the shape of a stance. Stand in the hollows and your feet will learn things." He has told it often. It is a good story, and you notice you have been standing in the stance he means.

choices.text: Ask him to show you the footwork

effects.log: He shows you, badly, and corrects himself. You correct him too, and neither of you can say how you knew.

choices.text: Buy him one more cup and listen

effects.log: He tells it three more ways. In all of them the stones are the same.

events.text: Yeom Bak's version: {llg_who} trained at {llg_thing} for sixty years without eating, cut a hill in half to see what was in it, and is still there, some nights, if you go and stand very quietly. People do go. They have worn a path. Some of them get better at fighting, from all that walking.

choices.text: Ask how far the walk is

effects.log: Nineteen days from anywhere, he says, and he means it as the good part of the story.

choices.text: Say it sounds like a good way to catch cold

effects.log: The crowd enjoys that. You catch sight of an old fighter in the back who is not laughing and is looking at your feet.

events.text: They say that all fighting began at {llg_thing}, in {llg_region}, when the first of the gods got into an argument with a boulder, and every school under heaven claims to come down from it. {llg_who} is the name they give to that god. In the capital, you hear, they have written six volumes on what the name means. In the village they sell it on bread.

choices.text: Buy the bread

effects.log: It is good bread. The stamp is a little figure in a stance. You look at the feet for a long time, and they are wrong.

choices.text: Ask who taught the god

effects.log: The baker laughs so hard he has to sit down. You had meant it as a real question.

events.text: A ballad is going round, "{llg_song}." "{llg_verse}," Yeom Bak sings. It is about {llg_who}, who he swears died at {llg_told_age} of {llg_cause}. You have not heard it before. You know how the next verse goes before he sings it, and when he gets it wrong, you wince.

choices.text: Sing the next verse with him

effects.log: You get it right, and he stops and stares. "Who taught you that?" You have no answer. He buys you a dumpling, warily.

choices.text: Keep your mouth shut and pay him

effects.log: It is a fine song. You hum it for a week and it does you no harm at all.

events.text: These days the Tale of {llg_who} takes three nights. On the first {llg_he} wrestles a flood. On the second {llg_he} marries, depending on the province, a princess or a tiger. On the third {llg_he} dies of {llg_cause}, at {llg_told_age}, and the whole teahouse cries. You cry too. It seems to you to be, on the whole, a very stupid story.

choices.text: Go back all three nights

effects.log: It costs you most of a week. The tiger is the best thing in it. You do not remember any tiger, and it is an odd thing not to remember.

choices.text: Ask Yeom Bak how much of it is true

effects.log: "All of it," he says, "by now." He seems to think this is an answer. In time you decide it is.

events.text: Grandmothers put children to sleep with it, and priests have opinions. {llg_who} made the moon out of something {llg_he} owed, and the fifth month has {llg_his} name in it, and no one would dream of saying that {llg_he} was ever one person, with a bad knee, in a province. It is your favourite story. You could not tell anybody why it makes your knee ache.

choices.text: Ask to hear the part about the moon again

effects.log: You fall asleep in the middle, as you are supposed to. You dream of a debt, and when you wake you have nearly got the sum.

choices.text: Say you are too old for that story

effects.log: The old woman telling it pats your hand. You are not too old for it, and you both know.

events.text: In {llg_region} they do it a certain way. They have done it so for {llg_years} years, they say: a turn of the wrist, three breaths before you start, the old count. Ask who started it, and you get a shrug. You watch them for a moment, and your hands are doing it already, behind your back.

choices.text: Ask them to show you

effects.log: They show you, and you do it better than they do. They think you must have had a teacher from there. You let them think so.

choices.text: Stop your hands, and walk on

effects.log: Your hands stop. Your hands are still thinking about it, though, and they go on thinking about it all that week.

events.text: Yeom Bak does not tell this one, as nobody has told it for a long time. There is only {llg_thing}, which people in {llg_region} do without thinking, and a saying that goes with it: "The way it was shown." Shown by whom? A very old woman frowns at you. Her grandmother knew, she says. It was somebody's grandmother's somebody.

choices.text: Ask her for the saying again

effects.log: You write it down. It means nothing at all. You read it often.

choices.text: Say that somebody must have thought of it first

effects.log: "I suppose so," she says, without interest. For some reason, you find this hard to bear, and then you find it funny.

events.text: Everyone does it, in {llg_region}. It is simply how it is done, like salt in soup. Scholars have proved it comes from the very beginning of the world. Nobody knows that it comes from anybody, and if you told them, they would be polite about it, and go on doing it. You catch yourself doing it wrong, and then correct it, and you have never been there.

choices.text: Try it the way they say to, on purpose

effects.log: It is, unfortunately, a very good way to do it. You do not know why that should make you so happy.

choices.text: Think about something else

effects.log: You do. Your hands, you notice, do not.

events.text: They do not say the name of {llg_who} in {llg_region} after dark. Yeom Bak will, for double, in a low voice: how {llg_he} held that country in {llg_his} fist, and how {llg_thing} is shut, and how no one has dared to knock it down in {llg_years} years in case it notices. Your stomach goes cold. You pay him the double.

choices.text: Ask what {llg_he} did

effects.log: They tell you a little. It's enough. You do not sleep well, and you would like very much to know why it feels like hearing your own name.

choices.text: Say it was a long time ago

effects.log: It was. Nobody thanks you for saying so, and you walk away more quickly than you meant to.

events.text: Every child in {llg_region} knows what {llg_who} will do if they do not come in at night. Yeom Bak's telling has more teeth in it than that. {llg_He} lived to {llg_told_age} on other people's years, he says, and there is a town with no one in it. You listen with a sick feeling, and find that you are checking the story for mistakes.

effects.log: It was. Nobody thanks you for saying so, and you walk away more quickly than you meant to.

events.text: There is a cold pass in {llg_region} that the maps call {llg_thing}. The carters will go a day around it. They say {llg_who} did something there, {llg_years} years back or more, to the people who lived under it. None of them say what. All of them look at the ground as they don't say it, and you do too.

events.text: The fighters' tale of {llg_who} has teeth and no thunder any more: where {llg_he} trained, what {llg_he} did to those {llg_he} trained, and how the ground at {llg_thing} is still kept clear because nobody wants to walk on it.

choices.text: Ask who was hurt by it

effects.log: A long list, they say. They give you three names, and the three names stay with you.

choices.text: Keep walking

effects.log: You keep walking. It does not make the road any shorter.

events.text: They still do it in {llg_region}, and now you hear what it was for. Someone with a long memory tells you that {llg_thing} began as a way of showing that you had paid {llg_who} what you owed. They have kept the gesture, and they have forgotten the fear.

effects.log: You keep walking. It does not make the road any shorter.

events.text: The gazetteer's entry on {llg_who} has been read aloud in the school at {llg_region} for some years now. It gives the dates, the age ({llg_age}) and the cause, {llg_cause}. It is the dullest thing you have ever heard. Yeom Bak's clapper can be heard through the wall, doing the dragon. You have the odd feeling that someone went to a lot of trouble to make this boring.

choices.text: Stay and hear the dates through

effects.log: You are the only one who stays. The teacher gives you a look of pure gratitude.

choices.text: Go next door and hear the dragon

effects.log: The dragon is excellent. He has had to work harder since the gazetteer. It has improved him.

events.text: A pilgrim cart comes through with a broken axle, on its way to {llg_region} to see {llg_thing}. You help them lift it. An old woman on the tailboard looks you over and pats the plank beside her. "You have the look," she says. "Come along. It's only a few weeks."

choices.text: Climb up

effects.log: The road takes its time. You do not ask yourself why you said yes.

choices.text: Wave them off

effects.log: The cart goes on without you. You watch it further than you need to.

events.text: A merchant needs someone to carry a sealed letter to {llg_region}, good pay, no questions. It is only when you have been thinking about it for most of a day that you realise that you meant to go there anyway, that you have been meaning to since you first heard about {llg_thing}.

choices.text: Take the letter

effects.log: The letter turns out to be a bill. You get paid regardless, and you are where you meant to be.

choices.text: Let someone else carry it

effects.log: Somebody else does. They come back and say that it is a fine road, and that you should see it some time.

events.text: You keep dreaming about {llg_landmark}, which you have never seen. It isn't a remarkable dream: you are climbing some steps, your knee hurts, you have something to do when you get there. You wake up cross, every time. This has been going on for a year.

choices.text: Go to {llg_region} and get it over with

effects.log: You pack in an hour. It feels less like setting out than like going back for something you forgot.

choices.text: Drink something before bed and stay where you are

effects.log: It helps, a bit. The knee goes on hurting in a way that the doctors find interesting.

events.text: Halfway up a hill in {llg_region}, a gate with no sect behind it any more, or a very small one: three teachers, some ducks, and sixty young people on {llg_thing}. Over the gate, in a hand you could not possibly know, is the first rule of {llg_house}. There is a bad joke hidden in it. They have been explaining it to each other, seriously, for {llg_years} years.

choices.text: Stand in the worn places

effects.log: Your feet go there without being told. Somebody with a stick shouts that you are doing it right, in a tone of real disgust.

choices.text: Watch the young ones first

effects.log: They have it nearly right. They have one thing wrong, and they have all got it wrong the same way, and you could tell them.

events.text: {llg_Thing} covers the whole of the hillside, with halls and stables and a street of shops to serve it. The gate would pass an army. The first rule of {llg_house} is cut over it taller than a person, and there is a bad joke hidden in that rule that nobody here has noticed in {llg_years} years. You laugh out loud in front of a thousand people, and you are stared at.

choices.text: Walk the old drill-lines at dawn, on your own

effects.log: No one has told you where they run. You finish at the place where you knew you would.

choices.text: Ask who keeps the place up

effects.log: A woman with a rake, it turns out, and she has heard every question you can think of. She lets you hold the rake.

events.text: In a small hall in {llg_region}, they still hold the morning count the way {llg_house} did it when someone you can't place kept the seat and kept it no better than it had been given. They added one thing, in those years: one slow breath before the bow. You breathe it with them, and you know exactly how bored that person was when they thought of it.

choices.text: Watch the old hands until they forget that you are there

effects.log: They do it without looking, the way you do your own buttons. You had not known that a thing could get so far from you.

choices.text: Offer a small correction

effects.log: They look at you. Then they look at the eldest, who tells you, kindly, that it has always been done this way.

events.text: All across {llg_region}, whole towns take that slow breath before they bow. It came down, they say, from {llg_house}, and they have made it into {llg_thing}, and it has outlived the hall it started in. Whoever first did it had been handed a seat they had not asked for, and only wanted a moment before the day began. You take the breath, and you want that moment too.

choices.text: Take a place at the end of the line, and try it

effects.log: A child corrects your elbow. You thank the child. You are, you find, a little bit in love with all of them.

choices.text: Ask why they do it

effects.log: They think about it honestly. "It works," they tell you, and that is the highest praise you have ever had.

events.text: A side-hall in {llg_region}, with a rank of tablets, the heads of {llg_house} in their order. Most are just names. One of them, {llg_who}, has a little dish of plums in front of it that nobody can account for. An old cook puts it out. "It has always been plums," the cook says. You have not eaten a plum in years. Your mouth is watering.

choices.text: Go in, and stand where the others stand

effects.log: You stand with your hands where theirs are. Nobody looks at you, and it is very quiet in your head, and it stays so for a while.

choices.text: Walk all the way round the outside first

effects.log: There is a door at the back that only someone who knew the mountain would have put there. You look at it a long time.

choices.text: Buy a stick of incense, like anybody else

effects.log: It costs next to nothing. You light it, and your hand does not shake, and you are rather proud of that.

events.text: {llg_Thing} was built for one head of {llg_house} among forty, and everyone agrees that it is too big. It has a plum tree in its court, and a rule that no one may raise their voice under it, since {llg_who} once sat under it and settled a war by being very tired. You put a hand on the bark. Whoever planted it had got the soil wrong, and it grew anyway.

choices.text: Ask the old sweeper what it was like before

effects.log: The sweeper has swept here for forty years and does not care to discuss it. There is a good deal to be said for that.

choices.text: Look at the face

effects.log: They got the face wrong, entirely wrong. You feel, of all things, relief.

events.text: A very small shrine by a ruined gate in {llg_region}, and one lamp in it, kept burning. {llg_house} fell once, and then a person came and raised it from the ash, and they have kept the lamp for that person ever since. The lamp is badly made. The boy who tends it says they have never let it go out. You find it hard, for a moment, to speak to the boy.

events.text: They have rebuilt the ruined gate twice over since, and {llg_thing} stands inside it now, with ninety-nine lamps. Whoever restored {llg_house} is on the wall in a dozen tellings, always with a broom, because they swept the ash out with their own hands. The first lamp is kept under glass, badly made and very small. There is a burn on your hand that has not been there before, or else you never noticed.

events.text: The village is called after {llg_house}, and half its people have the name, and not one of them is who you would have expected. They have the jaw, though. They have got it on a child throwing stones at a goose, and on the woman shouting at the child. A tree that somebody planted has become {llg_thing}, in a small way, on the hill. You sit down rather suddenly on the wall.

events.text: It has spread past the village now. There are towns of them, three market-days of them, all the way up to {llg_thing}, and the whole district has been called after {llg_house} for {llg_years} years. They have the jaw, ten thousand times over. A very rich man goes past in a chair, wearing it. You have to stop yourself from telling him to stand up straight.

events.text: The old drill field in the north is grazing land now. Sheep stand about on {llg_thing}. The earth banks are still there, and if you walk them you can see what they were for: someone who had been cold and frightened once, and knew just where the wind comes in. A shepherd sits in the lee of a bank, out of the wind, where someone put it for him {llg_years} years ago.

choices.text: Walk the old drill-lines at dawn, on your own

effects.log: No one has told you where they run. You finish at the place where you knew you would.

choices.text: Ask who keeps the place up

effects.log: A woman with a rake, it turns out, and she has heard every question you can think of. She lets you hold the rake.

events.text: {llg_Thing} is still in use. The frontier army trains here, as it has for {llg_years} years, on banks and lines drawn by {llg_who}, and every recruit learns the name as a swear word, and then, about the third winter, as something else. A sergeant is shouting at some boys. He is using a sentence that you made up. You would know it anywhere. It was unfair then, too.

effects.log: Your feet go there without being told. Somebody with a stick shouts that you are doing it right, in a tone of real disgust.

effects.log: They have it nearly right. They have one thing wrong, and they have all got it wrong the same way, and you could tell them.

events.text: There is a form that clerks in {llg_region} fill out, in triplicate, that no one has ever been able to explain. They call it {llg_thing}. Some long-gone official brought it in to stop one particular thief, and it stopped him, and the thief and the official are long forgotten. The clerk stamps yours. You know what the third copy is for. You are the only person alive who does.

events.text: Every magistrate in the empire works under the rule, and every candidate sits the question, and every peasant knows that you may take a dispute to the third gate. It is called {llg_thing} in {llg_region}, where it began. Nobody remembers it was one tired minister's idea, after one bad flood. Today you see it save a widow's field, in a quiet room. She thanks the magistrate. It is quite right that she should.

events.text: On a cliff above the road, in {llg_region}, someone has carved a shape: a person, and behind the person something very much larger. It is a poor carving. It was done by someone who saw it, or knew someone who did, and they could only say that it was tall. Pilgrims rub its foot for luck. You stop and look up, and between your shoulders you feel something shift its weight.

They have got the proportions badly wrong, and the size exactly right. Pilgrims come from the sea to walk its length. You stand at the small one's feet. You had thought that nobody else had noticed how big it was.

events.text: In {llg_region}, they say that if you tell a secret to a certain kind of noodle-seller, it will be in the capital by the new moon. Nobody remembers why it is true. {llg_who} set that up, or so says the Tale, with a string of cooks and a laundress. Your noodles come. The seller's eye goes to your hands, your boots and your purse, in that order. You taught them that order.

effects.log: Somebody's grandmother, they all say. Somebody's grandmother had a lot to answer for.

effects.log: They shout you down. The ending is the best part, and you had no right. You are delighted.

events.text: The Tale of {llg_who} is told in the capital in whispers: that {llg_he} knew what the Emperor had for breakfast, and who had poisoned it. Half the great houses claim to have outwitted {llg_him}. All of them still pay a nameless somebody, every quarter, in case. You are sitting in a teahouse. The boy who pours your tea has already told someone what you ordered. You would have fired him if he hadn't.

choices.text: Listen to all of it

effects.log: It takes the whole evening. They have got everything wrong, and you would not change a word, and you pay for a good seat.

effects.log: They take you to the spot. There are three of them, in fact, each with its own stall, and you buy a dumpling at the third.

events.text: A small bridge in {llg_region} is called Regent's Crossing, or {llg_thing}, by people who have no idea there was a regent. Somebody who sat in a seat that was not theirs built it, so as to have one thing to show for those years besides the keeping-warm of someone else's chair. It is a good bridge. You cross it. It was never going to be thanked, and it has carried carts for {llg_years} years.

choices.text: Climb it

effects.log: It takes a day, and it is an ordinary mountain, if you do not count your legs knowing the way.

choices.text: Ask at the inn how it came by its name

effects.log: You get a long answer, then a longer one from the next table. You buy both tables a drink before you can stop yourself.

events.text: The hill country they call {llg_thing} was a regent's gift to a child who grew up not to thank anyone for it. The records of the family barely mention the name of {llg_who}: a line, and a date, and "held the seat." The province, though, remembers who drained its marsh. An old woman is planting rice in a field that used to be water, and she tells you all about it, and gets the name wrong.

choices.text: Sit at the foot and look at it for a while

effects.log: People pass you and nod, the way you nod at someone doing what everyone does here.

choices.text: Read the boundary stone

effects.log: Your name, or a name, cut by someone in a hurry, and then worn by {llg_years} years of rain. You put your thumb in the first letter, and it fits.

events.text: Yeom Bak has one story he won't do in a hall with a roof: that for a generation in {llg_region}, the one on the seat was not the one who ruled. There was somebody in a back room, with a teacup. {llg_who}, if that's a name. Nobody can prove a thing. The tea, you notice, is still served in that house in a particular way, and you know why, because you liked it so.

You read their proofs in a back room with a cup of tea, and they are extremely good, and they leave out only the things that you personally arranged.

There's a stone in the outer wall of {llg_thing} with a chip in it that you made on another visit, in another body, when you were older and somebody else and had come here to find out what you felt. The incense is the same. The young sweeper is the old sweeper's great-grandchild, and sweeps exactly the same way.

It was you, of course, in a life ago that you can only half get hold of. You had paid in silver, and you had not signed it, and you are rather moved by your own tact.

effects.log: You check the rail and go down. It holds. You have, it appears, learned something at last.

effects.log: You knock the wedge back in with a stone. Nobody would ever know. That was, you remember, the point.

events.text: You have stood here before, in another life, and you remember the shame. Some of it, anyway, for that life seems to have worked at it. {llg_Thing} is still here, and a little less of it than you remember. Someone took some stones. You recognise the way the mortar's been cut: a thing that you yourself did, when you came here, wearing somebody else's name.

choices.text: Take another stone

effects.log: One stone. It takes all night. You carry it down yourself and leave it in the river.

choices.text: Go. You have done enough here, or you never will

effects.log: You do not settle which. You will come by here again, you suppose. Things like you do.

events.text: It comes on a wet night, on the steps, with no warning at all. You know how that wall was built, because you argued about it. You know the sound the third step makes. {llg_name}. That was your name: you lived {llg_age} years under it, and you died of {llg_cause}, and they are burning incense to you in there, and asking you for rain.

choices.text: Pick up a broom and say nothing

effects.log: The sweeper hands it over without comment. It is the first honest work anybody has done in your name for some time.

effects.log: You push the doors open. Everyone looks round. You have not, it turns out, thought about what happens next.

events.text: You are halfway up it when the mountain turns out to have a shape you know. There's the ledge where you ate your lunch. You were {llg_name}. They have called this whole height {llg_thing} after someone with your bad knee, your bad temper, and a death by {llg_cause}. Far below, you can hear someone giving directions by it. Turn left at you.

effects.log: It is a long way up, and you are not in a hurry. People will come this way who do not know whose stones they are stepping over.

effects.log: The first person you meet is selling turnips. You have, you realise, been waiting a very long time to say this to someone.

effects.log: The mason asks what to carve. You think about it for a while and tell him to carve the height.

events.text: A boy drops his guard in exactly the wrong way and you say, without thinking, "Left foot, you donkey." Everyone stops. It's what they call it here, the whole school: The Donkey Correction. Nobody knows why. {llg_name} knew why. You knew why. You lived {llg_age} years, and died of {llg_cause}, and your feet made these hollows. You had better say something.

choices.text: Say nothing. Show the boy the left foot

effects.log: The boy gets it on the fourth try. You will not tell him what he is standing in. You will just keep coming to look.

choices.text: Say that you made this place

effects.log: There is a silence. Then there is a laugh, and a big one. The biggest of them comes over to ask you to prove it.

choices.text: Tell them what the first drills were really for

effects.log: There is someone who writes these things down. They were for your knee, mostly. You will tell her that.

effects.log: The woman with the rake counts the silver twice. She says that it is about time someone did. You agree.

events.text: They have got to the part with your death in it, {llg_cause}, and everyone in the teahouse is crying, and the storyteller says the name. {llg_name}. And it arrives: a real room, a real bad smell, the actual last thing you said, which was about the soup. It was you. You were that small person with that bad knee. All this is about you. You can't stop laughing, and they are throwing things.

effects.log: You let the man finish. It is a good story. It belongs to them now, and you may as well enjoy it from the cheap seats.

effects.log: The room goes quiet. Yeom Bak turns round slowly. "Well, now," he says. "Come up here, friend, and tell us about the soup."

effects.log: Yeom Bak takes the silver. He takes none of your notes. It is by a long way the best thing that has ever been done with your money.

events.text: You see what it's for. They don't, and they have not for a long time. That turn of the wrist isn't the way of it at all: it was a way of hiding a shake, late on, when you were old, and were {llg_name}, and didn't want the young ones to see. The whole province does it. A little child is doing it now, in the road, without any shake at all, with enormous pride.

effects.log: It is a very small school. They ask what to call it. You tell them that it does not need a name, and they name it that.

You know because you had it built, and you were {llg_name}, and you remember now the sound it made shutting on people. You lived {llg_age} years. There are towns here that bolt their shutters to this day, and they are perfectly right. It's your hand on the wall, and it is not shaking. You would like it to shake.

Her mother smiles at you and says, "She's been very well brought up."

events.text: It has become a habit. You come when you can, and you sweep, and you mend what you can reach. A widow who comes on the first of each month has started saving you a rice cake. She tells you all about {llg_who}, whom she prays to about her son. She has it all wrong. Her son, she says, has lately started writing home. You think you may keep on with the sweeping.

choices.text: Eat the rice cake, and ask about the son

effects.log: You hear about the son for an hour. It turns out to be the most anyone has ever told you about yourself.

choices.text: Ask her what she would do if the god turned up

effects.log: "Tell {llg_him} off," she says at once. "For the state of the road." You mend the road.

events.text: Keeping up a mountain turns out to be mostly drains. You've cleared the path as far as the second ledge, and people have begun to call you the Path-Hand, and they don't give you a thought beyond that. Nobody up here knows you. Sometimes a child runs past you, shouting the name of the place, and the sound of it is a lot like being called in for dinner.

choices.text: Keep at the drains

effects.log: The spring rain goes where you tell it. It is very nearly the same thing as ruling a province, and much more peaceful.

choices.text: Teach a child how to set a stone

effects.log: The child is terrible at it, and then less terrible. Someone will be doing this after you, with no idea why.

events.text: You come back, year after year, and you never say what you are. You correct a foot, or a turn of the wrist, as though it's nothing. Some of the young ones have begun to watch for you. One of them asks, straight out, who you trained under. You've been thinking for some time what to say to that, and you find you still don't know.

choices.text: Say: "Nobody. You pick it up"

effects.log: It is not a lie, in the strictest sense. The young one nods gravely, and writes it down.

choices.text: Say: "Someone who got it wrong first"

effects.log: The young one thinks that over for a long time. You think that it may be the truest thing you ever taught.

events.text: You have learned the names, all you could get. You've dug a well for one village, under a false name, and paid off a debt in another. An old woman asks you why you do this. You tell her it's a vow. She looks at you for a long time and tells you that her people have a saying about vows, and about those who make them. She doesn't tell you what it is. She drinks from the well.

choices.text: Dig the next one

effects.log: Nobody forgives you, since nobody knows. It is, you begin to see, not that kind of a debt.

choices.text: Ask her what the saying is

effects.log: "It's very rude," she says, and she nearly smiles. It is more than you had coming.

events.text: You told them. There are still people here whose grandparents knew a person who knew {llg_who}, and they have got a test ready, since you are not the first to try: three questions. What did {llg_he} eat? Who was it {llg_he} never forgave? What did {llg_he} die of? An old woman leans forward to hear. It is plain that no one has ever got the second one right.

choices.text: Answer as only you could

ok.log: You answer. You say the name of the one you never forgave, and an old woman starts to cry, and asks you nothing further. They do not bow. They do, after that, always save you a seat.

fail.log: You answer, and you are right, and it makes no difference at all, because they have been telling it wrong for so long that the truth sounds like a very poor guess. They are kind about it.

effects.log: You say that you must have been drunk. Everyone is relieved, and so, to be honest, are you. It was a much better story when it was not about you.

events.text: You told them, and they brought you to the magistrate, who has a form for it. He has processed nine of you this year. There's one in the next room who's the Emperor. He asks you to prove it, kindly, in the tone of someone with a long afternoon in front of him. Behind him, a young fighter has come to stand in the door with her hand on her sword, wanting very much for it to be true.

events.text: You told them who you were. You had thought about being stoned, and you'd thought about being laughed at. What you hadn't thought of is this: they look at you, an ordinary person of no great size, and after a while, an old man says he supposes they should have you in and give you something to eat. Then he asks, quite politely, what you remember. He's got a brush.

choices.text: Tell him all of it

effects.log: It takes three days. He writes it all down and thanks you. He does not give you any more food. That seems fair, on the whole.

choices.text: Find that you cannot, and go

effects.log: You get as far as the gate. He does not call after you. He has been waiting a long time, and he is good at it.

events.text: Sim Haewon of the provincial gazetteers is a thin woman with ink on her cuff and no patience. She has spent nineteen years on the errors in the entry for {llg_who}. "Three of my predecessors went mad," she says, without looking up. Then she reads your list, and she looks up. "How do you know about the soup?" You had not put anything in about the soup. She has it in a footnote.

choices.text: Tell her it was handed down to you

effects.log: She does not believe it, and she writes it down anyway. "Oral source," she says. "Reliable, annoying." You work with her through the winter.

choices.text: Tell her the truth, and see what she does

effects.log: She considers you for some time. "I can't cite that," she says. "Sit down. Start with the dates." You have seldom been so happy.

events.text: Sim Haewon of the gazetteers reads your corrections to the Tale in silence, and then goes next door with them to Yeom Bak, who has been her enemy for thirty years. You can hear it through the wall. "There's no tiger?" "There was never a tiger, you fraud." "She says there's no tiger." Then they both come in and look at you. They have, you see, found the one thing they agree about.

choices.text: Say that there might have been a small tiger

effects.log: Yeom Bak weeps. Sim Haewon does not speak to you for a month. In her footnote it reads: "tiger (disputed)," and that is the finest thing anyone has ever written about you.

choices.text: Say there was no tiger

effects.log: Yeom Bak goes on telling it, and he is doing it now out of spite. It gets better. The entry is correct, and nobody reads it. Both of them say that you ruined their lives.

events.text: Sim Haewon doesn't want your account. "I have nine hundred pages from the people it was done to," she says. "What I lack is what it was like to decide." She dips her brush and waits. She has a very level way of looking at someone. It occurs to you that she has known for some time who you are, or what you are, and that she does not intend to make this any easier.

choices.text: Tell her what it was like to decide

effects.log: You tell her. It was easy, is the worst of it. She writes that down too. The entry is now the worst thing anybody has written about you, and it is all true.

choices.text: Tell her you cannot

effects.log: "No," she says, not unkindly. "Nobody can. Come back when you can." She leaves the page blank, with your name at the top.

events.text: The work goes on all that year: the drain they should have dug, the bad step, the roof. The master mason asks who's paying. A nobody, you tell him. He looks at the drawings you gave him, and at the old wall, and at you. "Same hand," he says. Then he shrugs: he's being paid. The monks hold a feast for the anonymous donor, and they give all the credit to {llg_who}.

choices.text: Go to the feast, and eat a great deal

effects.log: You are thanked by nobody and fed by everyone. You have certainly had worse deals from yourself.

choices.text: Carve something small where only you would look

effects.log: You leave it under the bottom step. If you come here again, you will know where to look.

events.text: The stone goes up at the top of {llg_thing}. It has only the height on it. Somebody will scratch a name on it within the month, and you know that. In the meantime, there's a very fine view from up there, of a whole province going about its business, not looking up. The mason's boy asks you whether you were related to anyone. You say that it's complicated.

choices.text: Sit up there until dark

effects.log: It was worth the silver. You would not have wanted the name on it now, anyway. You had not expected that.

choices.text: Scratch your own initials in it, and be first

effects.log: They are a new set of initials, and no one will ever work it out. It is an extremely childish thing to have done, and it makes your whole year.

events.text: The walls are up and the well is sweet. The school's got twice the students and half the sense. They've named the new hall for the donor, whom they imagine as a grateful old student of {llg_who}. On your last visit, the head of it asks you, very respectfully, whether you would care to watch them. You watch them. There's still something wrong with the left foot.

choices.text: Say nothing about the foot

effects.log: You keep your mouth shut. It is one of the hardest things you have ever done, in any body.

choices.text: Correct the foot

effects.log: It takes all morning. The head of the school goes pale, and then gets out a notebook.

events.text: Yeom Bak's new staging of the Tale opens on the first cold night, in a hall you paid for, with real snow, and he has used none of your notes. There is a tiger now, played by two men. Half of the town has come, and some of it has walked for days. In the third act, the figure with your name turns to the crowd and says something you never said, far better than anything you ever said.

choices.text: Take the line for your own from now on

effects.log: You start to use it. Nobody ever knows. You are, you find, not above stealing from yourself.

choices.text: Go round the back and tell him it was good

effects.log: He looks you over. "Of course it was," he says. Then he gives you the tiger's head to hold, and it is heavy and smells of glue.

events.text: The small school has eleven students. The eleventh has a shake in her hand, an old fever, and is ashamed of it. On the first morning, she sees how the turn is done, and goes very still, and you see it dawn on her that it could hide her shake. She looks up at you. You had not expected to be seen. You have waited {llg_years} years, it seems, for someone to get the joke.

choices.text: Nod, once

effects.log: You only nod. She goes back to work. You will find, some years on, that she is teaching it better than you.

choices.text: Show her what it was for

effects.log: You hold up your own hand and let it shake, and you hide it. She laughs till she has to sit down. It is the best day of two lives.

events.text: It goes up in a season and comes down in nine. Nobody helps at first. Then one morning, there is a boy, from the town with the shutters, who has come up and picked up a stone without asking what you're about. His father comes next. They don't speak to you. On the day the last of the wall is gone, the whole town walks up to look at the place, and it is only a hill. It is a very ordinary hill.

choices.text: Stand with them, and look at it

effects.log: Nobody says a word. Somebody passes round a water jar, and it reaches you, and they let it.

choices.text: Be gone before they come up

effects.log: You leave before the sun is up. Nobody ever knows who started it. The stones make a very good bridge, you hear.

events.text: You cannot pull down a mountain. You can, it turns out, pay a surveyor, and bribe a magistrate, and send a very boring petition up through nine offices for eleven years. The new map comes out in the spring. It gives the pass the name it had before, which an old woman had to remember for you. Nobody notices at first. Then a carter, for the first time, goes through by the short road.

choices.text: Go through by the short road yourself

effects.log: The carter nods to you. It is just a pass. The stream is very clear, and you drink from it, and you do not stay.

choices.text: Buy the old woman a meal, and tell her that it is done

effects.log: "I know," she says. "I can read." She lets you pay, though, and she has the expensive dumplings.

events.text: It takes longer than you would have thought. A thing like this doesn't come down at one blow. You have to talk to people, one at a time, and you must let some of them shout. Yeom Bak is furious, and then he's thoughtful, and then he has a new ending. It's a long time before you hear a child do it wrong, or say the old words in a new way, and have no one correct her. You stand there. Nothing happens. It's wonderful.

choices.text: Let it go at that

effects.log: You do not say anything. There will be no statue for this, and there is no one who could put one up.

choices.text: Tell the child she is doing it very well

effects.log: She gives you a suspicious look, and goes on as she was. Good.

events.text: A woman called Noh Ganeul turns up one autumn with a bundle and a walking stick. She goes from province to province seeing to the old places, she says, because somebody has to, and nobody pays her. She looks at what you have been doing to {llg_thing}, and she grunts, and asks you to hold the ladder. You hold the ladder. An hour later, she says, "You hold it as if you know how it fell the first time."

choices.text: Ask what she means

effects.log: "Nothing," she says. "People say things on ladders." She comes back through the next autumn. You find that you have been looking out for her.

choices.text: Go on holding the ladder

effects.log: You go on holding it. She comes down, pats the rung, and goes away. It is the most thorough looking-over you have ever had.

events.text: Noh Ganeul has brought a child with her this year: Dori, an orphan of some war or other, nine or so, who asks questions without stopping. "Who was {llg_who}? Was {llg_he} good? Why is it wrong? Who says?" Noh Ganeul has stopped answering them. Dori turns to you. "You know a lot about this place," Dori says. "Who was {llg_he} really?" There's no reason at all why that should be hard to answer.

choices.text: "Someone with a bad knee"

effects.log: "That's not in the story," says Dori, and thinks about it for a long time, and tells everyone. It is in the story now, in a small way.

choices.text: "Nobody knows. That is why you get to ask"

effects.log: Dori finds this a very poor answer, and says so. Noh Ganeul laughs for the first time in your hearing.

events.text: Noh Ganeul is getting too old for the walking. She sits down on the step of {llg_thing}, gets her breath, and tells you, not looking at you, that she has seen this before: every few generations, someone comes who knows the place too well. They mend things they couldn't know were broken. "I don't ask," she says. "My teacher didn't ask. Only don't die in the middle of the drains, it's a nuisance."

choices.text: Ask if the others found what they came for

effects.log: "They kept coming back," she says. "So, no. Or yes." She holds a hand out to be helped up. It weighs nothing.

choices.text: Promise you will not die in the middle of the drains

effects.log: She nods, as if this were a serious contract. You will find that you honour it.

events.text: A rich young man has come to see {llg_thing}, with his servants, a poet and a plan: he means to have it all gilded. He has the permits. Noh Ganeul stands in front of him with her stick and is ignored. He asks you, as the one who appears to work here, where the gilders should begin. He is, you notice, wearing a charm with the name of {llg_who} on it. He is very sincere.

choices.text: Tell him where the real rot is, and send his silver there

effects.log: The gilders do not come, but the carpenters do. He goes home happy, having been told that this is what {llg_who} would have wanted. You should know.

choices.text: Talk him out of it, kindly

ok.log: It takes you two days and most of a jar. He goes away thoughtful, and he leaves the poet, who turns out to be useful with a shovel.

fail.log: He has it gilded. It looks exactly as you had feared. Over the years, the gilt comes off in the rain, and Noh Ganeul sweeps it up and sells it.

events.text: Dori is grown, and doing the walking now. Dori comes up the path with the old stick and sits down beside you without a word, and it is some time before you understand that Noh Ganeul has died. She went in the middle of a road, which she'd have called a nuisance. Dori has got something for you. It's her list of the places, with one line against each. Against {llg_thing}, she has put: "In good hands. Don't ask."

choices.text: Walk the next stretch with Dori

effects.log: You carry the bundle as far as the river. It weighs a good deal less than you expected, and then a good deal more.

choices.text: Give the list back: Dori has the road now

effects.log: Dori takes it and nods. Dori has her way of nodding, exactly. You do not know whether to laugh, and you do both.

events.text: A broad man with a farmer's hands comes to see you. Gong Musan. His family has kept a reckoning for five generations, he says, and he has come to read it to someone, as the person who now tends {llg_thing} is the nearest thing to a responsible party. He sits down. He reads for three hours. It's all names and years. He never raises his voice. It is the most frightening thing that has happened to you in this life.

choices.text: Hear it through to the end, and ask for a copy

effects.log: He looks at you for a moment and makes you one, in his slow hand. It takes him a month. You keep it.

choices.text: Tell him that it was all a very long time ago

effects.log: "Yes," he says. He turns back to the first page and starts again. You have the rest of the day to think about what you said.

events.text: Gong Musan has worked it out, or enough of it. Nobody knows how. He comes up the road at dusk with a wood-axe, not hurrying, and says that he isn't a fool and that he doesn't know how such things can be, and that his grandmother told him what to look for. He says your hands are the same. He has come a long way. He sets the axe down on the ground, carefully, between you. He says that it's up to you.

choices.text: Kneel, and leave the axe where it is

effects.log: You stay on your knees until the moon is up. He picks up the axe, in the end, and goes home. It is the only time in five generations anyone has done that.

choices.text: Tell him what you have done with this life, and let him weigh it

ok.log: He listens. It does not balance, he says. He has done the sum. But he eats with you, in silence, and at dawn he leaves the axe behind.

fail.log: He hears you out. "That's the same voice," he says, and walks away from you. He leaves the axe. You cannot decide what that means, and you keep it.

events.text: Gong Musan's daughter has come instead. Her father has died in his bed, she says, of nothing in particular. She has the book. She's about twenty, and she has read it, and she's got a clear, untroubled face. "I'm getting married," she says. "I don't want this." She holds out five generations of names. "He said you'd know what to do with it." It's raining. Nobody has ever given you anything so heavy.

choices.text: Take the book, and let her go free of it

effects.log: She walks down the hill without looking back, and you are very glad of that. It goes on the shelf with the copy. You read it on the first of every month.

choices.text: Tell her it should go to the gazetteers

effects.log: She thinks about it, and nods. Sim Haewon receives it without comment. It runs to nine hundred pages, and now it is everybody's.

events.text: In the town with the shutters, they have started to leave one open. It's only the one, at the end of the street, on the bad night, and everybody pretends it's an accident. You go by, and an old man is sitting at the open window, with a lamp, looking at nothing, with an expression of enormous unconcern. He looks at you. You don't know what he knows. Your whole life, it seems, has been going past this one window.

choices.text: Nod to him, and walk on

effects.log: He does not nod back. On the way out of town you find you have been holding your breath for some years.

choices.text: Stop and ask if he needs anything

effects.log: "More oil," he says. He does not look at you. You bring it. It is the best-spent silver of two lives.

events.text: You are getting on, and the climb to {llg_thing} takes all morning. No one knows who you were. You have been a person with a broom, for a great many years, and they will bury you at the foot of the hill, near the drain, and someone will probably remember your cooking. It occurs to you that you've now done more for the place in this life than in the one it's named for.

choices.text: Do the steps one more time

effects.log: You sweep from the top down, the way that you always said to, and leave the broom where the next one will find it.

choices.text: Sit on the third step, and listen to it

effects.log: It still makes that sound. You could have fixed that, in either life. You are glad you did not.

events.text: They tell the story of you now, as well: the mad old person who came to {llg_thing} and said what they said. It's going into the Tale, as a comic interlude. Yeom Bak's successor came and asked you for the voice. You gave it. So now there's {llg_who}, and there's a person who said they were {llg_who}, and you're the only one who knows that both of them got the soup wrong.

choices.text: Correct the soup, one last time

effects.log: They write that in as well, with a laugh. It is a very good laugh.

choices.text: Let the interlude have the last word

effects.log: You find you have nothing to add. For you, that is a considerable event.

events.text: The gazetteer's new edition has come out, with the entry on {llg_who} in a sober half-page. It has your dates, your faults and the correct cause, {llg_cause}. Sim Haewon sent you a copy, with one word in the margin: "Adequate." No one will ever read it. Down the street, a child's getting the story wrong with tremendous energy. You keep the page by your bed. It's the first true thing anyone has said about you.

choices.text: Read it through again

effects.log: Yes, that is about the size of it. A small person with a bad knee. You sleep very well.

choices.text: Give the copy to the child down the street

effects.log: The child reads three lines and hands it back, disgusted. You have rarely been so proud of anyone.

events.text: What you built at {llg_thing} is old now too. There's moss on it, and somebody has got the story of how it was built wrong. You came here to check the drain, and it's fine. Whoever walks in here next will take it all for one thing, and one age, and one person's doing. They will be nearly right. You have left the place a bit stronger than you found it, twice. You wonder whom it'll be, the next time.

choices.text: Leave a note for the next one, under the bottom step

effects.log: "The drain is fine. Check the rail." You think that you will probably find it funny.

choices.text: Go home and leave it to them

effects.log: You go down without looking back. They will work it out, or they won't. You did.

events.text: You are old. You've done what you've done, in both of the lives, and you have stopped trying to make the sum come out. It doesn't. {llg_Thing} still has its name, and the people here still say it the same way. The difference is that you say it too, now, every morning, like a person taking something bitter that is good for them. You find it's a strange kind of peace, and you don't think you've earned it.

choices.text: Go on saying it

effects.log: Every morning, then. That is how much there is. You begin to be able to bear the mornings.

choices.text: Ask that you be buried with no marker at all

effects.log: They look at you oddly and agree. It is the one thing in either life that you have ever asked to be left out of.

events.text: There is nothing on the spot now. There is grass growing, the same as anywhere. Some young people came up last spring to have a picnic, and they had no idea. You can't say what you feel. You've come a long way to stand on nothing. It's no victory, but your hands have stopped doing what they used to do, in the night. You take off your shoes, for some reason, and you stand on the grass.

choices.text: Stay until the picnickers come back

effects.log: They offer you a dumpling. You take it. It is an ordinary dumpling, on an ordinary hill.

choices.text: Walk down barefoot

effects.log: It hurts, a bit. You are old. You get home with sore feet and sleep like a child.

events.text: You have not been back for some years. It's still there, you hear: {llg_thing}, in {llg_region}. Someone was telling it wrong at the inn only last week. You didn't correct them. Then you got up and paid for the whole table, for reasons you kept to yourself, and went out into the cold feeling better than you'd any right to.

choices.text: Walk home the long way

effects.log: The long way goes by the river. It is a fine night, and you are not in any hurry.

choices.text: Go back in and hear the end

effects.log: They have got as far as the tiger. You sit down again and buy another round.
